deep.reconstruction:
Layout: four blocks of 50 rows each, x = 6.850 to 7.150 in steps of 0.002. Each row gives:
- the argument x;
- an angle v(x) in degrees, minutes and seconds, with 5 decimals of the second;
- the first difference D(x) = v(x+0.002) - v(x), in arcseconds;
- the second difference D(x-0.002) - D(x), in units of 1e-5 arcsec.

The second-difference figure at the head of each block is carried over from the preceding block. The page joins seamlessly to fol. 194 (which ends 6.750-6.786 on the transcription) and fol. 196 (which starts at 7.150).

Additivity checks (my verification), e.g.:
- 147°41'13.07864" + 195.27305" = 147°44'28.35169".
- 148°57'37.27024" + 186.46264" = 149°0'43.73288".
- 195.27305 - 194.89541 = 0.37764, entered as 37764.
- 7.148: 154°44'17.93278" + 147.91088" = 154°46'45.84366".

Identification of the function (mine; the page carries no heading): with sigma = tan(v/2), the table satisfies
  x = log10[ 2 rho'' (sigma + sigma^3/3) ],  where rho'' = 206264.806".
Equivalently, sigma + sigma^3/3 = 10^x / (2 rho'').

This is the parabolic (Barker) equation tan(v/2) + (1/3) tan^3(v/2) ∝ t. Here v is the true anomaly and the argument is the common logarithm of the 'mean motion' quantity M = 2(sigma + sigma^3/3), expressed in arcseconds. So the page is a high-precision (about 11 significant figures) table of v as a function of log M for motion in a parabola. It is equivalently a table for solving the cubic sigma^3 + 3 sigma = 3M/(2 rho) via an angle.

Test at x = 7.000, v = 151°28'50.46916":
- psi = 180° - v = 28°31'9.53".
- sigma = cot(psi/2) = 3.93473, so sigma + sigma^3/3 = 24.2407.
- Times 412529.6 this gives about 1.0000006e7, i.e. log10 = 7.0000000.

The same fit holds at 6.852 and 7.148 to the accuracy of hand checking.

Derivative check (mine). Since dM/dv = rho (1 + sigma^2)^2,
  dv/dx = ln10 · 2(sigma + sigma^3/3) / (1 + sigma^2)^2  (radians per unit x).
At x = 7 this gives 0.41093 rad, i.e. 169.52" per step of 0.002. This matches the mean of the tabulated differences, (169.67791 + 169.36221)/2.

The smooth second differences (37859 decreasing to 26597) show the table was either built or checked by differences. That is Gauss's standard procedure for a master table that would later be rounded.
errors: None found. All entries spot-checked (including every place where the transcription has [?]) satisfy v(x+0.002) = v(x) + D(x) exactly, and the second differences agree with the first differences.

Several entries in the image visibly show overwritten or corrected digits, e.g. 44'28.35169", 186.81944, 185.39745, 6'55.59123", 13'6.03279", 40'33.40871". The corrected values are internally consistent.

results.what: High-precision table of the true anomaly v in a parabolic orbit as a function of log10 of M = 2 rho''(tan(v/2) + tan^3(v/2)/3), for v from about 147.7° to 154.8°, with first and second differences
results.modern_name: Barker's table / inversion of Barker's equation for parabolic motion (equivalently, the real root of the cubic s^3 + 3s = c)
results.usually_credited_to: Barker (1757) for the parabolic table; Euler, Lambert, Olbers and Gauss (Theoria Motus, 1809) for parabolic-motion methods

results.what: Construction or verification of a table by systematic first and second differences
results.usually_credited_to: Briggs, Mouton and the general practice of 17th-18th-century table makers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine (if unusually precise) computational table for parabolic motion, which is standard astronomical material and well within Gauss's known practice. The only mildly notable feature is the 11-figure precision and the log-argument format, which suggests a master table.
